notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 28, drawn from the sources found.

---

## Ezekiel 28:1–10 — The Prince of Tyre

**v. 1: "The word of the LORD came to me"** — This continues the series of oracles against Tyre (Ezekiel 26–28). Earlier chapters addressed the city; now God turns to its ruler. The historical figure is likely Ithobal II (Ethbaal II), who reigned ca. 590–573 BC during Nebuchadnezzar's siege. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 2: "Your heart is proud … 'I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea'"** — The core charge is pride. The prince regarded himself as divine, enthroned among the gods. His island fortress seemed impregnable, and Tyre's commercial empire gave him a sense of invincibility. Ellicott notes this is the "insanity of prosperity" — the king did not necessarily demand formal worship like later Roman emperors, but had that proud self-sufficiency that amounts to practical deification. Gill adds that this prince is "a lively type of antichrist" who "shows himself, and behaves, as if he was God" (2 Thessalonians 2:4). (biblehub.com/ellicott; mail.biblehub.com/gill; enduringword.com)

**v. 3: "Behold, you are wiser than Daniel"** — Spoken ironically. Daniel had been in Nebuchadnezzar's court for about 20 years by this point and was famed throughout the Babylonian Empire for wisdom and interpreting secrets (Daniel 1:20; 2:48; 4:18; 5:11–12). The prince of Tyre fancied himself even wiser. Ellicott observes that Daniel was "a classic example of a man whose head was not turned by his success" — the exact opposite of the Tyrian ruler. (biblehub.com/ellicott; enduringword.com)

**v. 4: "By your wisdom and understanding you have gained your wealth"** — God does not condemn the prince for possessing riches or even for being shrewd in trade. The problem is his response to those riches. Tyre's wealth came through maritime commerce and its strategic location, and the king credited his own wisdom rather than God. Gill notes the parallel with antichrist, who "by carnal policy, and hellish subtlety, has amassed vast treasures." (enduringword.com; mail.biblehub.com/gill)

**v. 5: "Your heart has grown proud because of it"** — Wealth "puffed up" the prince's heart. This is the central diagnosis: success in trade led to hubris. Constable comments, "It is not uncommon for people today, even Christians, to deify themselves in their own minds when they experience great success." (studylight.org/dcc; enduringword.com)

**v. 6–7: "I will bring foreigners against you, the most ruthless of nations"** — The judgment fits the crime: the one who claimed deity will meet the true God in battle. "If the prince has the audacity to claim prerogatives of deity, then let him prepare for a direct confrontation with the divine Lord of history" (Block, cited by Guzik). The "strangers" are the Babylonian (Chaldean) forces. Poole calls them "a foreign people, called strangers for their multitude." (enduringword.com)

**v. 8: "They will bring you down to the Pit … die a violent death in the heart of the seas"** — The "Pit" is the grave, Sheol. Tyre's location "in the heart of the seas" — once its boast — becomes the scene of its death. Ellicott notes the plural "deaths" in the Hebrew, indicating an emphatically violent death. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

**v. 9: "Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who slay you?"** — A bitter sarcasm. Before his executioners, the prince's pretensions to deity will evaporate. "Gods do not die; humans do" (Vawter & Hoppe, cited by Guzik). Gill applies this to antichrist: when taken and cast into the lake of fire, he "will not have the impudence to style himself God." (enduringword.com; mail.biblehub.com/gill)

**v. 10: "You will die the death of the uncircumcised at the hands of foreigners"** — The Phoenicians practiced circumcision, so to die as "uncircumcised" meant to die a shameful, barbarian's death — utterly disgraced. Constable compares it to the death described in 1 Samuel 17:26, 36 regarding Goliath. (studylight.org/dcc; biblehub.com/ellicott)

---

## Ezekiel 28:11–19 — The Lament for the King of Tyre

**This section is the most debated in the chapter.** There are three main interpretive positions:

1. **Satan only** — the passage describes the fall of Satan using Tyre's king as a starting point (Chafer, Unger, Pentecost; common in classic dispensationalism).
2. **The human king only** — the language is figurative, mythological, or hyperbolic, describing the king of Tyre in Eden-like imagery (Alexander, Block, Stuart, Constable, Allen).
3. **Both the human king and Satan** — the earthly king typifies or is indwelt by the spiritual power behind him, similar to the "prince of Persia" in Daniel 10 (Feinberg, Cooper, Dyer, Ryrie, Guzik, Wiersbe). This is the majority traditional Protestant view.

(studylight.org/dcc; bible.org/seriespage/3-satan-s-fall — search excerpt; enduringword.com)

---

**v. 11: "Again the word of the LORD came to me"** — A new oracle begins, now a "lament" (funeral dirge). The Hebrew word for "king" (melek) is used here rather than "prince" (nagid) in v. 2, which some argue signals a shift to a different referent. Others say it is the same person viewed from a different angle. (studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 12: "You were the seal of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty"** — "Seal of perfection" (literally "the one sealing a plan," per Constable) means the king was the consummation of Tyre's glory, the one who affixed his seal to the plans producing Tyre's maritime success. Those who see Satan here argue this describes a being far greater than any earthly king — a created angel of supreme wisdom and beauty. Ellicott takes the whole passage as "strongly ironical." (studylight.org/dcc; biblehub.com/ellicott; enduringword.com)

**v. 13: "You were in Eden, the garden of God. Every kind of precious stone adorned you …"** — The traditional Satan reading: Satan was in the actual Garden of Eden (cf. Genesis 3, the serpent). The nine gemstones parallel those on the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17–20), suggesting a priestly role. The LXX inserts all twelve stones. The human-king reading: "Eden" is figurative for the king's blessed, prosperous state. Alexander (cited by Constable) suggests an alternative — ancient Near Eastern temples typically had garden enclosures, and "Eden, a garden of a god" may be a metaphor for the temple complex of Melkart, Tyre's patron deity. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc; mail.biblehub.com/gill)

**"The workmanship of your timbrels and pipes was prepared for you on the day of your creation"** — The Hebrew for "timbrels and pipes" is difficult. Some translations render it "settings and mountings" (for the gems). The traditional Satan reading takes it as musical instruments, suggesting Satan had a role in heavenly worship music (cf. Job 38:7). Gill notes that music was prepared for the king of Tyre's coronation, and likewise for the pope of Rome at his "creation and inauguration." (enduringword.com; mail.biblehub.com/gill)

**v. 14: "You were anointed as a guardian cherub … on the holy mountain of God … among the fiery stones"** — 

**Traditional (Satan) reading:** This is the strongest evidence for a superhuman referent. Satan was "the anointed cherub who covers" — one of the exalted angelic beings guarding God's throne (cf. the cherubim over the mercy seat, Exodus 25:20). "The holy mountain of God" is the heavenly Zion (Hebrews 12:22). "Fiery stones" may refer to the seraphim ("burning ones," Isaiah 6:2) or the brilliant gemstones of the heavenly realm. Guzik: "Satan, before his fall, was one of the privileged angelic beings surrounding the throne of God." Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary states plainly, "this covering cherub … seems definitely to point to Lucifer, almost totally personified in the king of Tyre." (enduringword.com; studylight.org/ghb)

**Human-king reading:** Constable argues the king was "cherub-like" — God had allowed him to reign as a guardian over Tyre. "Holy mountain of God" may be figurative for a kingdom (cf. Psalm 30:7) or a reference to the king walking in Jerusalem among fiery stones after its destruction. Alexander (cited by Constable) notes that the Phoenician male-sphinx (cherub) was bejeweled and sometimes had the head of a priest-king, so the imagery draws on Phoenician religious culture rather than making an ontological statement about Satan. (studylight.org/dcc)

**Ellicott's view:** The imagery is borrowed from the Temple on Mount Zion — the prophet is speaking ironically of the king as if he were the anointed cherub over the mercy seat. The "stones of fire" allude to Exodus 24:10 where a sapphire pavement appears beneath God's feet with devouring fire. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

**v. 15: "From the day you were created you were blameless in your ways — until wickedness was found in you"** — 

**Satan reading:** Satan was created perfect and remained so until he fell. The iniquity originated from within him, not from God. 1 Timothy 3:6 warns against pride lest one "fall into the condemnation of the devil" — linking Satan's fall to pride. The bible.org excerpt states, "Satan, though perfect, sinned against God by becoming prideful and instigating a rebellion in heaven."

**Human-king reading:** The king had conducted himself well from his earliest days until pride overtook him — renewing "still more clearly the comparison with Adam" (Ellicott). The king was like Adam: prosperous until sin became manifest, then cast out. (biblehub.com/ellicott; studylight.org/dcc)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** adds: "Let it be expressly understood that the king of Tyre was born, not created … This leads to the seeming necessary inference that the devil was the person described, whom the king of Tyre typified." (studylight.org/ghb)

**v. 16: "By the vastness of your trade, you were filled with violence, and you sinned"** — 

**Satan reading:** The word "trade" or "traffick" (Hebrew rekullah) can also carry the sense of "going about for slanderous gossip" — Satan went among the angels spreading slander to incite rebellion, leading one-third of the angels to follow him (Revelation 12:4). This "violence" was his competitive, rebellious ambition (Isaiah 14:13–14). Guzik notes that the connection of Tyre's commercial sin to Satan shows "the devil can be in business just as much as in armies and war." (enduringword.com; bible.org/satan's-fall — search excerpt)

**Human-king reading:** The reference to trade is straightforward — Tyre's abundant commerce led to dishonest dealing, violence, and oppression. Constable: "The reference to trade supports the view that the earthly king is in view." (studylight.org/dcc)

**"I drove you in disgrace from the mountain of God … I banished you, O guardian cherub, from among the fiery stones"** — In the Satan reading, this describes his expulsion from heaven. In the human-king reading, God removed the king from his privileged place of rule. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 17: "Your heart grew proud of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor"** — All interpreters agree: pride is the root sin. In the Satan reading, this echoes Isaiah 14:13–14 ("I will ascend … I will make myself like the Most High"). The beauty God gave became the occasion of rebellion. God resists the proud (James 4:6). (enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 18: "By the multitude of your iniquities and the dishonesty of your trading you have profaned your sanctuaries"** — Tyre had many temples and was called "the Holy Island." The king's sin defiled these. In the Satan reading, his "sanctuaries" were the heavenly precincts he corrupted. "Fire from within you" — judgment arising from the sinner's own self. Ellicott: "the sin is represented as consisting in the abuse of the very blessings which God had given, and this sin as leading directly to its own punishment." (biblehub.com/ellicott; enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 19: "All the nations who know you are appalled … You have come to a horrible end and will be no more."** — The destruction is total, public, and final. Guzik notes this was fulfilled historically for Tyre (burned by Nebuchadnezzar, then by Alexander the Great) and will be fulfilled eschatologically for Satan. (enduringword.com)

---

## Ezekiel 28:20–26 — Judgment on Sidon and Restoration of Israel

**v. 20–21: "Set your face against Sidon and prophesy against her"** — Sidon was the older Phoenician city, about 25 miles north of Tyre. Ellicott gives four reasons for a separate oracle: (1) Sidon was the mother-city of Tyre and always independent, so might seem exempt; (2) Sidon had been the peculiar source of idolatrous influence on Israel — from the Judges period (Judges 10:6), through Solomon (1 Kings 11:33), and climaxing with Jezebel, daughter of Sidon's king and high priest of Baal (1 Kings 16:31); (3) Sidon's Thammuz worship still influenced Judah (Ezekiel 8:14); (4) Sidon had rejoiced in Jerusalem's fall. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

**v. 22: "I am against you, O Sidon, and I will be glorified within you"** — Constable (citing Klein) says this verse is the theological key to all the oracles against foreign nations: Yahweh vindicates His holiness and glorifies His name by judging the nations. (studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 23: "I will send a plague … blood in her streets; the slain will fall … the sword … on every side"** — Three judgments: pestilence, bloodshed, and the sword — the same triad found in Ezekiel 6:11–12 and 14:21. The goal is that "they will know that I am the LORD." (studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 24: "no longer face a pricking brier or a painful thorn from all around them"** — The language echoes Numbers 33:55, where God warned that the Canaanite nations would become "thorns in your sides" if Israel failed to drive them out. Sidon and the surrounding nations had been exactly that. Constable notes the reason for Sidon's judgment was "that Sidon had been a thorn in the side of God's people by scorning them (cf. Genesis 12:3)." (biblehub.com/ellicott; studylight.org/dcc)

**v. 25–26: "When I gather the house of Israel … they will dwell in their own land … build houses, and plant vineyards … dwell securely"** — A classic restoration promise, paired with the judgments on the nations (a pattern seen in Deuteronomy 30:3; Jeremiah 23:3; Ezekiel 11:17; 36:24). Ellicott says the immediate point is return from exile, but "this promise of rest looks forward in some sense to the final victory over all evil." Constable notes that after the Babylonian Captivity some Jews returned, but "the Jews have never yet lived safely in their own land. Fulfillment awaits the return of Jesus Christ and His millennial kingdom." Guzik: "God's plan for Israel as a nation is not finished." (enduringword.com; studylight.org/dcc; biblehub.com/ellicott)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### On whether vv. 11–19 refer to Satan

- **Dispensational / Pentecostal / many Baptists** (Chafer, Unger, Pentecost, Feinberg, Wiersbe, Guzik): The passage goes beyond any human king and gives the Bible's most detailed portrait of Satan's original glory and fall. Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary explicitly states: "This covering cherub … seems definitely to point to Lucifer." (studylight.org/ghb; enduringword.com)

- **Reformed / Covenant theology (some):** Many Reformed commentators also hold the Satan view (e.g., G. Campbell Morgan, cited by Guzik: "the most graphic and illuminating portrayal of Satan"). However, others are cautious, noting that the passage must first be read as addressing the historical king of Tyre before drawing typological connections.

- **Literal-human-king view** (Dr. Thomas Constable / Dallas Theological Seminary, and some evangelicals like Daniel Block, John Taylor, Ralph Alexander): The entire passage addresses the human king. Constable writes, "I think that neither Ezekiel 28:11–19 nor Isaiah 14 contains information about Satan before the Fall. The main reason … is that in both cases a king (of Tyre or Babylon) is the object of the prophecy. A literal interpretation of these 'kings' is possible and, therefore, preferable." (studylight.org/dcc)

- **Darby's Synopsis** (Plymouth Brethren / dispensational pioneer): "Verses 11–19, while continuing to speak of Tyre, go, I think, much farther, and disclose, though darkly, the fall and the ways of Satan, become through our sin the prince and god of this world." (biblehub.com/darby)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

**Dr. Constable's notes** (via studylight.org/dcc) cite Ralph Alexander's proposal that the imagery draws on Phoenician religious culture: the king of Tyre identified with Melkart, the city's patron deity, whose name means "king of the city." The bejeweled "guardian cherub" reflects the Phoenician male-sphinx (cherub), which was bejeweled and sometimes had a priest-king's head. "Eden, a garden of a god" may describe the temple complex of Melkart with its garden enclosure. The "fiery stones" may reflect the ritual burning of Melkart's effigy at his resurrection festival, known from a bowl found at Sidon. This cultural-hermeneutical approach interprets the passage without reference to Satan. (studylight.org/dcc)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

Gill's Exposition (a Baptist source) repeatedly draws parallels between the king of Tyre and the Pope as antichrist ("the whore of Rome," "the pope's triple crown"), reflecting historic Protestant polemic rather than Catholic self-understanding. Further searching on those specific sites would be needed for the Catholic/Orthodox perspective.

---

### Older Commentaries (non-aligned)

- **Gill**: Reads vv. 1–10 as primarily about the historical prince but with prophetic application to antichrist (the Papacy). Reads vv. 11–19 as describing the king but with language that surpasses him, hinting at Satan and again at antichrist. (mail.biblehub.com/gill)

- **Ellicott**: Treats the entire passage as strongly ironical — the king is compared to Adam in Eden, a "covering cherub" on the holy mountain — all deliberate hyperbole to heighten the shame of his fall. No Satan reference. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

- **Poole** (cited by Guzik and Ellicott): Takes "strangers" in v. 7 as the Babylonian forces. Explains the gemstones of v. 13 in detail (sardius = red/ruby; topaz = yellowish green; diamond = clear/sparkling; beryl = sea-green; onyx = white like a fingernail; jasper = various colours, best green; sapphire = sky blue; emerald = green with golden spots; carbuncle = flame colour). (enduringword.com)
